description: The concentration field is one of the macroscopic variables used in the derived equations, serving as a quantified field in the continuum description of chemotaxis.
Bacterial density is the other macroscopic field incorporated into the derived equations, enabling quantitative description of population-level chemotactic behavior.
The derived macroscopic equations describe and capture the nonlocal response of the bacterial chemotaxis system.
The modeling framework explicitly incorporates the slow methylation process through the macroscopic equations, which are derived to represent its effect on chemotactic dynamics.
In the study context, Escherichia coli experiences chemotactic regulation governed by slow methylation of chemoreceptors, which shapes its response to chemical gradients.
Escherichia coli is the organism in which the chemotaxis pathway is studied as the canonical sensory system, making the bacterium the biological context for the pathway.
The signal transduction module is one of the two core modules that constitute the chemotaxis pathway architecture.
The adaptation module is the second core module within the chemotaxis pathway and works alongside signal transduction to produce chemotactic behavior.
The signal transduction module detects changes in environmental conditions and amplifies those signals for downstream behavioral control.
The signal transduction module carries out the signal transduction process by detecting, amplifying, and transmitting environmental signals.
Rapid transmission of signals by the signal transduction module leads to control of bacterial swimming behavior.
After initial stimulation, the adaptation module resets the activity and sensitivity of the signal transduction module, thereby modulating its response dynamics.
The adaptation module implements the adaptation process by gradually restoring pathway responsiveness after stimulation.
Adaptation enables temporal comparisons by resetting pathway activity and sensitivity after initial stimulation.
Temporal comparisons are necessary for bacterial chemotaxis and thereby support appropriate swimming behavior in changing environments.

The interplay between the signal transduction and adaptation modules shapes the quantitative features of the chemotaxis pathway, with adaptation modifying the effective response of signal transduction over time.
The interplay between the pathway's two modules gives rise to multiple quantitative emergent properties described in the abstract.
The emergent quantitative features are interpreted in the context of evolutionary optimization of chemotactic behavior, serving as the basis for rationalization rather than a direct measurement.
